newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Dec 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Dec 20.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- RECEIVER SEEKS BUYER FOR DEBT-HIT DUNN AND CO

Dunn and Co, the high street men's wear retailer, has gone into receivership. Accountancy firm KPMG have been appointed to the company which has debts of more than six million stg. Problems arose because of a decline in the formal wear market.
Paul Jeffery, of KPMG, said that it was his intention to run the stores as normal while carrying out a full review of the business.
-- ACCELERATING MONETARY GROWTH FUELS RATE RISE CALL

Building society indicators suggest that the recovery in the housing market remains on course despite a dip in home loan advances. This comes as a fresh surge in money supply revived calls for an early rise in interest rates. Bank of England figures suggest there was a further acceleration in monetary growth last month with money supply expanding faster than at any time in six years.
-- COACH OPERATOR SHERINGS TO BE SOLD TO BUYOUT TEAM

Rank, the leisure giant, has announced the 83 million stg sale of the coach holiday operator, Sherings, to a buyout team backed by NatWest Ventures. Sherings is the second business to be sold by Rank chief executive Andrew Teare after the 72 million stg disposal of Precision Industries in September. Rank has also announced that it is selling its Kingston Plantation resort in South Carolina for 30 million stg and its high street amusement arcade business for 25 million stg.
THE TIMES
-- HALIFAX SPENDING A LITTLE EXTRA 413 MILLION STG ON FLOTATION

The Halifax Building Society has revealed it will become the thirtieth biggest bank in the world at a cost of 413 million stg, which will mean 46 pounds stg for every borrower and saver. 260 million stg of costs will be associated with the Leeds Building Society merger and 153 million stg in conversion expenses, including fees to lawyers and merchant bankers.
-- DELAY ON PAYOUT TO LLOYD'S NAMES

Lloyd's of London has admitted it faces delays in paying out funds under its recovery plan. It admitted that about 4,000 Names will have to pay more to settle their dues at Lloyd's due to adverse movements in the currency exchanges and denied that the delays threaten a knock-on effect in the insurance market.
Chief executive Ron Sandler has written to Names to apologise for setbacks to the payment timetable and said that no effort was being spared to bring the process back on track.
-- ASDA ASDD.L KEEPS IT SIMPLE AND VERY PROFITABLE

Chairman of Asda and Conservative Party prospective parliamentary candidate for Tumbridge Wells, Archie Norman, has said that the supermarket group will not follow its rivals into financial services and loyalty cards and will stick to the business of "simple" shopkeeping. He said that real success lies in concentrating on fresh food, value for money and service. Asda is testing a loyalty card in twenty stores but has no plans to introduce it nationwide due to its high cost.
THE GUARDIAN
-- LABOUR LAYS DOWN LAW ON COMMODITY MARKET REFORM

Shadow economic secretary Mike O'Brien has warned that a Labour government could strip the London Metal Exchange of its right to operate as a self-regulatory body unless the City's biggest and most powerful commodity market embraces reforms demanded by the Securities and Investment Board watchdog. The news comes as SIB unveiled the findings of a six-month investigation into the running of the City's commodity markets.
-- GALLAHER AXES 950 JOBS IN CHESHIRE RUN-DOWN

The international tobacco company, Gallaher, has provoked fury by announcing the run-down of its factory in Cheshire, with the intention of closing it in the year 2000, with the loss of 950 jobs. The announcement was made without consulting union officials and the company will receive 9.9 million stg in government funding towards a 45.6 million stg expansion of its plant in Northern Ireland, which will create 290 jobs.
-- VAUXHALL BUYS BACK INTO VANS

Vauxhall is set to join forces with Renault in a 180 million stg project, which will create 900 jobs in Britain and re-establish the manufacturer in the van market. The deal will involve IBC Vehicles, which is 82 percent owned by General Motors, Vauxhall's US parent. Production of the van will not start until the turn of the century, and in the meantime Renault will supply IBC with its Traffic model.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- EUROSTAR'S ONE BILLION STG FLOATATION ON TRACK AS TRAFFIC RETURNS

Preparations will begin early next year for a one billion stg floatation of London and Continental Railways, the Eurostar train operator. This follows the quicker than expected recovery from the Channel Tunnel fire, with passenger numbers likely to be back to normal levels by January. The proceeds from the floatation will be used to fund the construction of the 2.8 billion stg Channel Tunnel high-speed rail link into London's St Pancras station.
-- US COURT TELLS GKN TO PAY OUT 331 MILLION STG

One of the UK's biggest car-parts groups, GKN, has been ordered by a US court to pay up to 554 million dollars in damages in a dispute over its American car-exhaust business. The company and analysts were surprised by the extent of the award, which could wipe out its cash reserves and hit this year's final profit figures. Shares fell sharply after the news. The action was brought by small garage owners who operated franchises for Meineke Discount Muffler Shops, GKN's retail car-exhaust chain.
-- BSKYB WARNED TO PLAY FAIR ON DIGITAL TELEVISION

Telecommunications regulator Don Cruickshank has announced new guidelines for the multi-channel television era which will curb any attempts by BSkyB, Rupert Murdoch's satellite channel, to unfairly control digital television services to viewers through its set-top box technology. He promised to stamp out any discrimination between Sky programmes and the offerings of other broadcasters. Cruickshank's powers could be watered down if British Telecom wins a legal challenge over similar powers.
